title: SPLADE: learned sparse retrieval
summary: SPLADE keeps the inverted index of a word search engine but lets a model decide the weights, including weights on words the document never contained. One index instead of two, paid for in longer posting lists. Measured on this course's real index: 3,894 terms and 15,424 postings today, and the cost of expansion is linear in the expansion factor.
html:
The last three days built a two engine system. A word index for exact strings, a vector index for meaning, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion to glue the two result lists together. It works, and the obvious complaint is that you now run and maintain two indexes.

SPLADE asks a different question. What if you keep just the word index, and teach a model to write better words into it?

The idea in one example

A word index is a table. For every word, a list of the documents containing it, with a weight per document. Day 32's BM25 computes those weights by counting.

Take a document that says "the mortgage rate dropped". BM25 gives it entries under three words: mortgage, rate, dropped. That is all it can ever match on.

SPLADE produces something more like this:

mortgage  2.4
rate      1.9
dropped   1.2
interest  1.1     not in the document
loan      0.8     not in the document
fell      0.7     not in the document
housing   0.5     not in the document

Same table, same structure, same inverted index, but four of those seven words never appear in the text. Now a search for "interest rates fell" matches this document by plain word lookup, with no embeddings anywhere. The semantics got baked into the index at write time.

The analogy: BM25 indexes the words the author actually wrote. SPLADE indexes the words a careful editor would have pencilled into the margin so that people could find it.

Where the extra words come from

From a model that was trained to fill in blanks. Give a BERT style model the sentence "the mortgage rate ____" and it produces a score for every word in its 30,000 word vocabulary: "dropped" high, "fell" high, "exploded" lower, "banana" near zero. That machinery already exists and it already knows which words belong near which.

SPLADE runs that over the whole document, collects the scores across the vocabulary, keeps the large ones and throws the rest away. The survivors, with their scores, are the index entries.

The catch, which is a storage problem

Left alone, the model puts a small nonzero score on thousands of words per document. That is a disaster for an inverted index, because the cost of answering a query is the cost of walking the posting lists for the query's words, and those lists just got much longer. Taken to the limit, every word's list contains every document, and you have built the slowest possible way to scan everything.

So SPLADE's training includes a penalty for using too many words. That penalty is the real knob, and it trades quality directly against index size and query latency. Not a tuning detail, the central design decision.

There is a second cost that gets less airtime: queries get expanded too. Your three word query becomes fifteen or twenty terms, so you walk more lists as well as longer ones. Both multipliers apply at once.

If you want to see it measured

I cannot run SPLADE in this container, so what follows is real measurement of the base and honest arithmetic on top of it. Here is the actual inverted index over the 34 lessons of this course:

documents            34
distinct terms    3,894
total postings   15,424
per document        454 distinct terms, 1,128 tokens
average list        4.0 documents

query "overlap between chunks"          3 terms,  32 postings walked
query "how many bytes does one vector"  7 terms, 174 postings walked

Now the arithmetic. If each document expanded to twice its distinct terms, total postings go from 15,424 to about 31,000 and that first query walks 64 postings instead of 32. At four times, 62,000 postings and 128 walked. Expansion cost is linear in the expansion factor, on both the storage side and the query side.

Be clear about what that is and is not. The index numbers are measured. The expansion factor is assumed, because I did not run the model. And at 34 documents the absolute counts mean nothing. What transfers to a real corpus is the shape: doubling the terms per document doubles your index and doubles your posting walk, and that is a cost you pay on every query forever in exchange for a one time quality gain.

Is it worth it

On the public benchmarks SPLADE beats BM25 consistently and often beats single vector dense retrieval. That is the reported result and I have not reproduced it. Three things worth holding alongside it.

Indexing now needs a model pass over every document, so ingestion needs a GPU and your reindex time goes up by orders of magnitude. Query time needs a model pass too, to expand the query. And the benchmark papers tend to lead with the quality number and bury the latency number.

Whether SPLADE beats a dense index fused with BM25 for your system is not settled. The honest version is that it depends on whether you already run a lexical engine, because if you do, SPLADE is a change of weights in a system you already operate, and that is a much easier sell than a second database.

If you remember one thing
SPLADE puts the semantics into a word index by letting a model add words the document never contained. You keep one inverted index, and you pay for it in longer posting lists on every query.

Tomorrow closes out phase 2 with ColBERT, which goes the other way: instead of one vector per document it keeps one per token, and compares them all against all.
exercise:
One. Write your day 35 note.

Two. Think about the identifier problem from day 33. If SPLADE's model expands SKU-4417 into nearby vocabulary, does the identifier still match exactly, or do you get the same smoothing failure in a new place? Write down your guess, then one sentence on how you would test it with an index you control. This is a genuinely open question for most teams running SPLADE and nobody checks it.
